title: Someone is shouting at you in public
lede: A stranger, a customer, or a neighbour has raised their voice at you in a shop, a street, or an office. People are watching. Your face is hot and your hands have started to shake.

blocks.text: A stranger, a customer, or a neighbour has raised their voice at you in a shop, a street, or an office. People are watching. Your face is hot and your hands have started to shake.

items: Volume is a bid for control, not a prelude to violence in most cases. The shouter wants you to lose composure so the exchange becomes symmetrical.
The audience is not judging who is right. It is judging who is more regulated. This is the one contest you can reliably win.
Matching their volume moves you into their frame, where they have more practice than you.
Your shaking hands are adrenaline, not fear of them, and they are invisible to almost everyone watching.

items.move: Take four seconds before your first word
items.detail: Breathe out longer than you breathe in. It physically slows your heart and buys you the only thing you need: a sentence chosen rather than fired.

items.move: Drop your volume rather than raising it
items.detail: Speak slightly quieter than normal. It forces them to lower theirs to hear you, and it signals to the room who is in control.

items.move: Increase distance without turning your back
items.detail: A step back, an angled body, a counter between you. It reduces threat perception on both sides.
Not "calm down" — that is petrol. Describe: "You are shouting. I want to help and I cannot do it at this volume."
Choice restores their sense of agency, which is usually the thing they came in missing.

items.move: Set a boundary with a consequence you will actually carry out
items.detail: Never bluff. If you say you will end the conversation, end it.

items.say: "I hear that you are angry, and I do want to sort it. Talk to me at a normal volume and I will start now."
"Two options: I fix it here in five minutes, or I get my manager. Which would you rather?"
"I am going to step away for a minute. I will come back and we will finish this."
Say nothing about the insult. Repeat the practical sentence, unchanged, once.

items: "Calm down." It has never worked once in human history.
Smirking or the flat customer-service smile. It reads as contempt and escalates fast.
Explaining policy at length while they are still hot. Nothing is being absorbed.
Winning in front of an audience. A humiliated shouter escalates rather than retreats.
Log it the same day: time, words used, witnesses. Repeat offenders are only ever dealt with on the strength of a paper trail.
Discharge the adrenaline physically — walk, stairs, cold water on the wrists. Suppressed adrenaline becomes a headache and a bad evening.
Tell one person out loud what happened. It stops the incident replaying at 2am.
Ask yourself only one question: was there a real fault underneath the volume? Sometimes there is.

limit: If they close distance, block your exit, mention a weapon, or follow you when you disengage, this is no longer a conflict — it is a threat. Leave toward people, call for help, and stop trying to resolve it.
